Who Writes the Rules: Codes, Standards, the AHJ, and Listing

Unit 2: Codes and Standards. Lesson 8 of 52 in INST1 Academy.

The inspector walks into the TR, points at a cable, and says it has to come out. You say the standard allows it. He says the code does not. Who wins? You need to know the difference before you argue.

Code versus standard

A code is a rule adopted into law and enforced by an inspector. The NEC is a code once your jurisdiction adopts it. A standard is a consensus document that sets the technical method. It is not law by itself, but it becomes binding when a code, a contract, or a specification calls for it.

The AHJ

The authority having jurisdiction is the inspector, the fire marshal, or the building official whose decision wins on your job. Mounting heights, permit rules, and whether a product is acceptable are the AHJ's call. Local codes may be stricter than the national ones, and the stricter rule applies.

Document            What it governs
NFPA 70 (the NEC)   wiring, cable listings, bonding, and firestop of penetrations
Building and fire   construction, fire ratings, and means of egress
codes
OSHA                jobsite safety for workers
TIA-568             cabling topology, distances, performance, and tests
TIA-569             pathways and spaces
TIA-606             administration and labeling
TIA-607             bonding and grounding
ISO/IEC 11801       the international structured cabling standard

Listing

A product is listed when an NRTL, such as UL, has tested it for a stated use and put it on a published list. The label on the product is how you and the inspector know it. A product listed for one use is not automatically acceptable for another.

When documents disagree

Ask the designer in writing. The stricter requirement wins, and the AHJ settles anything unclear.

Tip: keep the listing label or the jacket print visible until the inspector has passed the work.
Exam tip: a standard becomes enforceable when a code or contract calls for it, and the AHJ's decision overrides your reading of any document.
Remember
A code is law, a standard is consensus until a contract or code adopts it, the AHJ decides, and a listing proves a product was tested.
Deeper explanation

Who Writes the Rules: Codes, Standards, the AHJ, and Listing, explained slowly

Who wins when documents disagree

Most disputes on a job come from the same question: who has the final word? The order below settles most of them. The stricter document usually wins, and when it does not, the AHJ decides.

Source                 Force          Example
Adopted code           the law        the NEC after your state adopts it
AHJ ruling             binding        the inspector's decision on a firestop
Contract and spec      binding        the cabling category the owner ordered
Standard               guidance       the TIA standard when no contract calls for it
Manufacturer           warranty       the listed installation instructions

A standard turns binding when a code, a contract, or a specification calls for it. A specification that says "install per the TIA-568 standard" makes the standard part of your contract.

Listing versus labeling

A product is listed when an NRTL (UL is the best-known one) tests it and puts it on a published list for a stated use. The label on the product shows that listing. A cable listed as CMR is not acceptable for a plenum. A firestop system is listed for a certain wall and penetrant, and not for another.

Worked example

The drawing shows one outlet height. The AHJ says accessibility rules require a different one. Your own habit says a third. Three sources, three answers. The AHJ's rule wins, because mounting heights and permit rules are the AHJ's call. You document the conflict, ask the designer to update the drawing, and mount to the AHJ's height.

Examples of what each family covers

Question                         Document family
What does the cable need to be?  TIA-568
How big and where is the TR?     TIA-569
How do I label it?               TIA-606
How do I bond it?                TIA-607
What cable rating in the plenum? NEC (NFPA 70)
What PPE do I wear?              OSHA

What to do

When you do not know which governs, ask the foreman and the designer in writing. Write down the AHJ's answer, with the date and the person's name.

Remember: codes are law, standards bind through contracts, the AHJ decides, and the stricter rule wins.
